conventions.convention: Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, ⟨u,v⟩ = conj⟨v,u⟩, ⟨v,v⟩ ≥ 0 with ⟨v,v⟩ = 0 iff v = 0; conjugation is the identity in the real case, the induced length is ‖v‖ = sqrt(⟨v,v⟩), and every statement is written once and read in either scalar field.

Completeness of a Hilbert space is Cauchy-sequence completeness of the induced norm (it is a Banach space for it), explicitly not sigma-completeness of decreasing closed sets; the closest-point, Riesz, orthogonal-decomposition and adjoint layer is stated under the Axiom of Countable Choice, and the page records that the Cauchy-complete form is the one that spends it.

For a nonnegative family over an arbitrary index set I the sum is the supremum of its finite subsums in [0,+∞]; a scalar family is summable when its finite-subset net over Fin(I) ordered by inclusion converges; ℓ²(I,F) is defined by this convention and nothing in the definition asserts completeness. No enumeration, ordering or countability of I is assumed.

An orthonormal indexed family satisfies ⟨e_i,e_j⟩ = δ_ij; its closed linear span is the smallest closed subspace containing it; the family is complete (a complete orthonormal system) when that span is H, and a Hilbert basis is a complete orthonormal family; the empty family is complete exactly for H = {0}. It is not a Hamel basis, carries no order, and partial sums are indexed by finite subsets.

The torus is T = R/Z with the quotient topology and the normalized translation-invariant Borel (Haar) measure represented on [0,1); T^n is handled by finite products with m(E) = λ_n(q^{-1}[E]), characters are e_k(x) = exp(2π i k.x) and Fourier coefficients are f-hat(k) = integral of f against e_{-k}.

A linear map T between normed spaces over the same field is compact when the closure of T(A) is compact in Y for every bounded A; the closed unit ball suffices, and compactness implies boundedness (boundedness is not a hypothesis of the definition).

A Fredholm operator is a bounded T with finite-dimensional kernel, closed range and finite-dimensional cokernel Y/ran T as an algebraic quotient; the index is dim ker T minus dim coker T, and closedness of the range is an explicit hypothesis while the cokernel dimension is the vector-space dimension of the quotient.

For a bounded operator on a complex Banach space, ρ(T) = {λ : λI − T is bijective with bounded inverse}, σ(T) is the complement, eigenvalues are scalars with nonzero kernel, the point spectrum lies in σ(T), and the resolvent is R(λ,T) = (λI − T)^{-1}, matching the Banach-algebra resolvent R(z,a) = (z1 − a)^{-1}; only complex scalars are treated.

f(T) for a bounded normal T on a nonzero complex Hilbert space is the unique isometric unital star-isomorphism C(σ(T)) → C*(I,T) with z mapping to T (for self-adjoint T the same map is produced by the polynomial isometry), and the Borel calculus is f(T) = Φ_E(f) against the unique regular spectral PVM E with integral of z dE = T; the two agree on continuous functions.

A projection valued measure assigns to every measurable set an orthogonal projection with P² = P = P*, E(∅) = 0, E(X) = I, E(B ∩ C) = E(B)E(C), and strong countable additivity E(B)x = sum_n E(B_n)x in norm; regular means X is locally compact Hausdorff with the Borel sigma-algebra and every finite positive measure E_x(B) = ⟨E(B)x,x⟩ is regular; E_{x,y} = ⟨E(·)x,y⟩ are the complex measures integrated against, with the pairing linear in the first variable.

Positive (for a bounded self-adjoint operator) means ⟨Tx,x⟩ is a real number in [0,+∞) for every x, and S ≤ T is defined only for self-adjoint S,T by ⟨(T − S)x,x⟩ ≥ 0; the order is a partial order on the real vector space of self-adjoint operators, and dropping self-adjointness invalidates the order calculus.

Numerical range is defined for nonzero H by W(T) = {⟨Tx,x⟩ : ‖x‖ = 1} with w(T) = sup{|z| : z ∈ W(T)}; the zero Hilbert space carries the explicit library convention W(0) = {0} and w(0) = 0, so a zero-dimensional compression has a singleton numerical range rather than the empty set.

Existence of a maximal orthonormal set uses full AC once through Zorn's lemma, and that same AC supplies the Countable Choice hypothesis of the Parseval layer; the Hilbert-basis statement records that full AC is the declared hypothesis and is spent exactly once.

Hilbert–Schmidt data are relative to a Hilbert basis E supplied as data: s_E(T) = sum_{e in E} ‖Te‖² is the finite-subset supremum in [0,+∞], T is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to E when s_E(T) < +∞, and then ‖T‖_{HS,E} = s_E(T)^{1/2}; when the sum is +∞ no HS norm is defined.

For a nonzero separable Hilbert space the multiplicity function is read off a fixed finite-or-countable cyclic decomposition with common dominating measure μ = sum_j 2^{-j}(1+μ_j(σ(T)))^{-1} μ_j and m(z) = #{j : h_j(z) > 0}; its a.e. class and the measure class of μ are asserted independent of the decomposition, and the zero Hilbert space is a separate trivial class with empty spectrum and no PVM.

load_bearing.statement: A real or complex inner-product space is an F-vector space with a pairing that is linear in the first argument, satisfies ⟨u,v⟩ = conjugate of ⟨v,u⟩, ⟨v,v⟩ ≥ 0 and ⟨v,v⟩ = 0 iff v = 0, and carries the induced length ‖v‖ = sqrt(⟨v,v⟩); conjugation is the identity in the real case, the pairing is conjugate-linear in the second argument, and the page convention fixes linearity in the first argument.

A real (resp. complex) Hilbert space is a real (resp. complex) inner-product space whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence for ‖v‖ = sqrt(⟨v,v⟩) converges in the space, so it is exactly a Banach space for the induced norm; completeness is the Cauchy-sequence notion, explicitly not sigma-completeness.

An indexed family (e_i) is orthonormal when ⟨e_i,e_j⟩ = δ_ij; its closed linear span is the smallest closed subspace containing every e_i; the family is complete when that span is H, a Hilbert basis is a complete orthonormal family, and the empty family is complete exactly for H = {0}.

For a nonnegative family (c_i) over an arbitrary set I, sum_{i in I} c_i is the supremum of the finite subsums in [0,+∞]; a scalar family is summable when its finite-subset net over Fin(I) ordered by inclusion converges, and ℓ²(I,F) is the set of families with finite square sum, with ‖a‖₂ = (sum |a_i|²)^{1/2}; the definition asserts no completeness.

A linear map T: X → Y between normed spaces over the same field is compact when the closure of T(A) is a compact subset of Y for every bounded A; equivalently when the closure of the image of the closed unit ball is compact, and every compact operator is bounded.
For all vectors x,y in a real or complex inner-product space, |⟨x,y⟩| ≤ ‖x‖‖y‖, with equality if and only if x and y are linearly dependent.
Assume Countable Choice. For bounded operators between real or complex Hilbert spaces: (aR+bS)* = conj(a)R* + conj(b)S* and the adjoint is unique; (TS)* = S*T*; T** = T and ‖T*‖ = ‖T‖; ‖T*T‖ = ‖T‖².

Assume Countable Choice. For T in B(H): T is self-adjoint when T* = T; positive when ⟨Tx,x⟩ is a real number in [0,+∞) for every x; unitary when T*T = TT* = I; normal when T*T = TT*; the definitions are read over either scalar field.
Vectors x,y are orthogonal, written x ⊥ y, when ⟨x,y⟩ = 0; for a subset S the orthogonal complement is S^⊥ = {v : ⟨v,s⟩ = 0 for every s in S}, a linear subspace with {0}^⊥ = V and V^⊥ = {0}.

For T in B(X) on a complex Banach space, ρ(T) = {λ in C : λI − T is bijective and its inverse is a bounded operator}, σ(T) is the complement, eigenvalues are the scalars with nonzero kernel, and the generalized eigenspace at λ is the union of the kernels of (T − λI)^n; the resolvent is R(λ,T) = (λI − T)^{-1}.

Assume Countable Choice. A PVM E on a measurable space (X,Σ) assigns to every B a projection with E(B)² = E(B) = E(B)*, E(∅) = 0, E(X) = I, E(B ∩ C) = E(B)E(C), and strong countable additivity E(B)x = sum_n E(B_n)x in norm for pairwise disjoint B_n with union B; it is regular when X is locally compact Hausdorff with the Borel sigma-algebra and every E_x(B) = ⟨E(B)x,x⟩ is a regular Borel measure.

For an orthonormal family (e_i), a finite F and P_F x = sum_{i in F} ⟨x,e_i⟩e_i: P_F x lies in the span and ‖P_F x‖² = sum_{i in F}|⟨x,e_i⟩|²; the residual x − P_F x is orthogonal to that span; ‖x − P_F x‖² = ‖x‖² − sum_{i in F}|⟨x,e_i⟩|², hence the finite Bessel inequality sum_{i in F}|⟨x,e_i⟩|² ≤ ‖x‖²; and P_F x is the unique best approximation from that span.

For bounded T: X → Y between Banach spaces over the same field, T is Fredholm when ker T is finite dimensional, ran T is closed, and the cokernel Y/ran T (algebraic quotient) is finite dimensional; the index is dim ker T − dim coker T, with subtraction in Z.

For Hilbert spaces H,K over R or C with pairing linear in the first argument, T in B(H,K) of norm ‖T‖, and a Hilbert basis E of H supplied as data: s_E(T) = sum_{e in E}‖Te‖² (finite-subset supremum in [0,+∞]); T is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to E when s_E(T) < +∞, and then ‖T‖_{HS,E} = s_E(T)^{1/2}.

Assume AC. For a bounded normal operator T on a nonzero complex Hilbert space there is a unique isometric unital star-isomorphism C(σ(T)) → C*(I,T), f ↦ f(T), sending the coordinate function z to T; for self-adjoint T it agrees with the self-adjoint calculus.

Assume Countable Choice. For a PVM E on (X,Σ) and x,y in a complex Hilbert space: E_x is a positive measure with E_x(X) = ‖x‖² and 0 ≤ E_x(B) ≤ ‖x‖²; E_{x,y} is a finite complex measure, linear in x and conjugate-linear in y, with E_{y,x} = conjugate of E_{x,y}; |E_{x,y}|(X) ≤ ‖x‖‖y‖; and E_{x,y} = (1/4) sum_{k=0}^{3} i^k E_{x+i^k y} as complex measures.

Assume Countable Choice. For a bounded measurable f: X → C and a PVM E on (X,Σ) with H nonzero: there is a unique Φ_E(f) in B(H) with ⟨Φ_E(f)x,y⟩ = ∫ f dE_{x,y}, obtained as the norm limit of integrals of uniformly convergent simple approximations and independent of the approximating sequence; ‖Φ_E(f)‖ ≤ ‖f‖_∞, ⟨Φ_E(f)x,x⟩ = ∫ f dE_x and ‖Φ_E(f)x‖² = ∫ |f|² dE_x; the exact norm is the E-essential supremum over unit x.

the norm ‖T‖ = sup over the closed unit ball, used in the adjoint identities, compactness and the HS norm layer
the space B(X,Y) and B(H) in which all resolsolvent, compactness and functional-calculus statements live

the definition of a completion (Banach space, linear isometry, dense image) used by thm-completion-of-an-inner-product-space-is-hilbert

completeness of L^p (and of L² on the torus and of the direct-sum model in the multiplicity definition)
the representative-independent complex L² pairing ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫ f conj(g) with Cauchy–Schwarz, used by the kernel and convolution layers
existence and uniqueness of the orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace of L²(μ), used by the concrete L² projection material
identification of the product integral with iterated integrals for nonnegative product-measurable functions, used in the square-integrable kernel items
the L¹ Fubini theorem, used to justify the kernel operator's section integrals
representation of bounded functionals on C_0(X) by unique finite regular complex Borel measures with ‖L‖ = |μ|(X), the key input to the regular-PVM construction
uniqueness of Radon measures from equality of integrals on C_c, used for uniqueness clauses of the spectral PVM
positive functionals on C_0(X) have finite regular representing measures with μ(X) = ‖L‖, used in constructing the regular spectral PVM
density of C_c(X) in L^p(μ) for a Radon measure and 1 ≤ p < ∞, used in the cyclic-spectral-representation layer
uniform density of point-separating self-adjoint complex function algebras, used for spectral permanence and the positivity/Gelfand arguments
positivity as a = b*b and normality a*a = aa* in a C*-algebra, used by spectral permanence and the positive square root
ambient-algebra spectrum σ_A(a) and resolvent R(z,a) = (z1 − a)^{-1}, matching the operator resolvent convention of this group
characters (nonzero multiplicative linear functionals) and the character space Δ(A) with the pointwise-evaluation topology, used throughout the Gelfand construction
the Gelfand transform is an isometric unital star-isomorphism of a nonzero unital commutative complex C*-algebra onto C(Δ(A)); used by spectral permanence and the normal functional calculus
σ_A(a) = {χ(a) : χ in Δ(A)} with |χ(a)| ≤ r(a) ≤ ‖a‖ for a nonzero commutative unital complex Banach algebra; used by the generated-algebra character space and spectral mapping
r(a) = ‖a‖ for a normal element of a unital complex C*-algebra; used by cor-normal-operator-norm-equals-spectral-radius and the polynomial isometry
χ(a*) = conjugate of χ(a); used by spectral permanence and by thm-positive-square-root (whose nonnegativity of χ on positive elements takes the one extra line χ(b*b) = |χ(b)|²)

Δ(A) is nonempty, compact and Hausdorff for a nonzero commutative unital complex Banach algebra, with the weak-star description of the topology; used by spectral permanence and the character-space homeomorphism

concerns.concern: The closing sentence 'it is a different operator from the Banach transpose T-prime whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear' compares the Hilbert adjoint T*: K → H with the transpose T-prime: K* → H*, which have different domains and codomains, so 'different operator' is not a well-typed comparison; the preceding identity R_H T* = T-prime R_K is what carries the content, and the sentence supplies no criterion a reader can check.

Well-definedness clause (7) asserts that the measure class of μ and the a.e. class of m are independent of the chosen cyclic decomposition while deferring to the intertwiner lemma and the classification theorem later on the same page; the definition's data are fixed by a choice, and the item that is supposed to justify the independence is stated through those same data, so a reader cannot verify the claim from the definition alone and the organisation invites a circularity objection (I traced the uses and found no actual circular dependence, but the claim is asserted rather than derived in place).
